notes.explanation: The SEC says SEC and FINRA rules require this disclosure.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Opening an Options Account (updated 16 July 2026)
notes.evidence: your broker must provide you with a copy of a publication from the Options Clearing Corporation called “Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options.”

notes.front: What must happen before a customer can trade options?
notes.back: The broker must approve the account for options trading, using the customer’s options agreement.
notes.explanation: The broker judges from the agreement whether options suit the customer, and which types.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Opening an Options Account (updated 16 July 2026)
notes.evidence: Before you can trade options, your broker must approve your brokerage account for options trading. In order to be approved for options trading, you will need to fill out your broker’s options agreement.

notes.front: Under Rule 9b-1, who prepares the options disclosure document?
notes.back: One or more options markets, which file it with the SEC.
notes.explanation: Amendments and supplements form part of the document.
notes.evidence: Options disclosure document means a document, including all amendments and supplements thereto, prepared by one or more options markets which has been filed with the Commission

notes.front: An investor wants a debt security paid from the principal and interest on a large pool of home loans. What is it?
notes.back: A: a mortgage-backed security.
notes.choices:
A) A mortgage-backed security
B) A debenture
C) A Treasury bill
notes.choicesExplained: B: a debenture rests on one company’s general credit. C: a T-bill is a short-term Treasury obligation, not a claim on loans.
notes.explanation: An MBS represents claims to the cash flows from pooled mortgage loans.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Mortgage-Backed Securities and Collateralized Mortgage Obligations”
notes.evidence: Mortgage-backed securities (MBS) are debt obligations that represent claims to the cash flows from pools of mortgage loans, most commonly on residential property.

notes.front: A retailer sells 7-year debt securities to investors to fund new stores. Investors get interest and their principal back, but no stake in the firm. What are they?
notes.back: C: corporate bonds.
notes.choices:
A) Common stock
B) Municipal securities
C) Corporate bonds
notes.choicesExplained: A: common stock would give an ownership interest. B: municipal securities are issued by states and local governments.
notes.explanation: Companies issue corporate bonds to raise money, promising face value at maturity and usually interest until then.
notes.evidence: With a bond, the company promises to return the face value of the bond, also known as principal, on a specified maturity date. Until that date, the company usually pays you a stated rate of interest, generally semiannually.

notes.front: A company has callable 7% bonds outstanding, and rates on its new debt have fallen to 4%. What is it most likely to do?
notes.back: A: call the bonds and refinance at the lower rate.
notes.choices:
A) Call the 7% bonds and borrow again at the lower rate
B) Raise the coupon on the 7% bonds
C) Leave the bonds alone because calls are only allowed when rates rise
notes.choicesExplained: B: calling saves the issuer money, while a higher coupon would cost it more. C: issuers may call when rates drop below the bond’s rate.
notes.explanation: Calling when rates fall lets the issuer save money.
notes.evidence: An issuer may choose to call a bond when current interest rates drop below the interest rate on the bond. That way the issuer can save money by paying off the bond and issuing another bond at a lower interest rate.

notes.front: A depositor holds two CDs of $150,000 each, both in her name at the same federally insured bank. How much of the $300,000 is insured?
notes.back: $250,000: the limit covers all her accounts at that bank, not each CD.
notes.explanation: The limit applies across all accounts in one name at one bank.
notes.evidence: The $250,000 insurance covers all accounts in your name at the same bank, not each CD or account you have at the bank.

notes.front: Using the SEC’s bands, how is a corporate bond maturing in seven years classed?
notes.back: C: medium term (four to 10 years).
notes.choices:
A) Short term
B) Long term
C) Medium term
notes.choicesExplained: A: short term is under three years. B: long term is more than 10 years.
notes.explanation: The SEC bands maturities as short, medium or long.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: What Are Corporate Bonds? (4 June 2013)
notes.evidence: Maturities can be short term (less than three years), medium term (four to 10 years), or long term (more than 10 years).

notes.front: A new customer wants to place an options order today, but has not yet received the options disclosure document. What must the broker-dealer do?
notes.back: B: furnish the document before accepting the order.
notes.choices:
A) Accept the order and mail the document later
B) Furnish the document first; until then it may not accept the order
C) Accept the order if the customer signs a waiver
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule bars accepting the order until the document is furnished. C: the rule’s condition is furnishing the document, not a signature.
notes.explanation: Rule 9b-1 ties both account approval and order acceptance to furnishing the document.
notes.evidence: No broker or dealer shall accept an order from a customer to purchase or sell an option contract relating to an options class that is the subject of a definitive options disclosure document, or approve the customer's account for the trading of such option, unless the broker or dealer furnishes or has furnished to the customer a copy

notes.front: What does Rule 10b-18 give an issuer that repurchases its own common stock?
notes.back: A voluntary safe harbour from manipulation liability based on the manner, timing, price and volume of its repurchases.
notes.explanation: Compliance is voluntary.
notes.evidence: issuer (and its affiliated purchasers) with a “safe harbor” from liability for manipulation under sections 9(a)(2) of the Act and § 240.10b-5 under the Act solely by reason of the manner, timing, price, and volume of their repurchases

notes.front: How many Rule 10b-18 conditions must an issuer’s repurchases meet each day, and what if one fails?
notes.back: Four; failing any one removes all of that day’s repurchases from the safe harbour.
notes.explanation: The conditions apply on a daily basis.
notes.evidence: To come within the safe harbor, however, an issuer's repurchases must satisfy (on a daily basis) each of the section's four conditions. Failure to meet any one of the four conditions will remove all of the issuer's repurchases from the safe harbor

notes.front: Rule 10b-18 purchases on any single day must not exceed {{c1::25 percent}} of the security’s average daily trading volume (`ADTV`).
notes.explanation: That volume is measured over the four calendar weeks before the purchase week.
notes.evidence: The total volume of Rule 10b-18 purchases effected by or for the issuer and any affiliated purchasers effected on any single day must not exceed 25 percent of the ADTV for that security
